Julie Haney is a Computer Scientist in the Visualization and Usability Group at the National Institute of Standards and Technology. She leads the NIST Human-Centered Cybersecurity Program and conducts research about the human element of cybersecurity and privacy. Previously she spent over 20 years working at Department of Defense as a cybersecurity professional and technical leader. She earned a Ph.D. in Human-Centered Computing from University of Maryland, Baltimore County. She has a B.S. in Computer Science from Loyola University Maryland and an M.S. in Computer Science from University of Maryland.

Breaking: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens.
  • In a recent development, to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models.
  • In a recent development, today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

In a recent development, to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

In a recent development, today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

Recent findings suggest that JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

In a recent development, LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):.

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

In a recent development, the role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

According to recent reports, in short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

In a recent development, LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the latest vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Sources indicate that tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data.
  • In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project.
  • It has been revealed that today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with upcoming AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data. That is why preparing high-quality training and evaluation data comes first. Fine-tuning an open-weight model, running reinforcement learning, or building an evaluation suite all depend on data that is accurate, well-labeled, and representative of your task. For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model customized on clean, task-specific data can often match or exceed the accuracy of a larger general-purpose model prompted into shape, at a lower cost per inference.

In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project. Labeled examples are scarce or expensive, and privacy rules limit what you can use. Quality problems such as duplicates, label noise, and answer leakage go unnoticed until a training run disappoints, and every training technique expects data in its own format. As a result, data scientists spend weeks wrangling data instead of building models.

It has been revealed that today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with upcoming AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. You work in your notebook or IDE, with specifications and code that you can inspect and change.

With AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block. You can use one of them on its own or chain them together according to the workflow you want.

According to recent reports, you work wherever you already work. Use the SageMaker Python SDK directly or provide your coding agent the AI-ML skill in the agent toolkit and let your agent invoke the APIs according to established data science best practices. Describe what you need, and the agent selects and runs the right capability in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab, Kiro, or your local IDE with your coding assistant of choice.

For teams building specialized models, the hardest part is often finding enough task-specific data. Splunk, a Cisco company, faced exactly this when building evaluation models for its Agent Observability product.

Industry observers note that “For Splunk Agent Observability, our ability to train robust GenAI Eval models relies on access to high-quality, diverse datasets which are hard to curate for very specific tasks. Amazon SageMaker AI data preparation capabilities for synthetic data generation is meaningfully helping us scale these capabilities. We’ve been able to generate statistically representative synthetic datasets reliably and fast, while preserving the underlying patterns our models depend on. The seamless integration with the rest of our SageMaker workflow means our data scientists and customers spend less time wrangling data and more time building models that drive real enterprise value through Splunk.”.

— Yash Sheth, Director of Engineering, Splunk Agent Observability.

Recent findings suggest that the value grows when you combine the capabilities. Some common patterns:.

In a recent development, build a golden evaluation dataset: Auto-label your raw data from a small seed set. High-confidence rows are accepted automatically, and low-confidence rows go to human reviewers. Their corrections improve the next labeling pass, resulting in a trusted, human-validated dataset to benchmark your models against.

Go from raw documents to a trained model in one workflow:.

Consider a team preparing data to evaluate agentic customer support assistants. Its product guide claims that a factory reset erases saved settings. The team wants to test whether the assistant preserves that warning when answering reset questions.

One pass through the preparation workflow looks like this:.

This example workflow illustrates how the capabilities fit together.

With the AI-ML skill, you describe the task in natural language while your coding agent helps build specifications, prepare code, and coordinate the data preparation steps. You can open those artifacts to see how the workflow is configured and make changes directly.

According to recent reports, if you prefer to invoke the APIs yourself, use the Python SDK APIs to call individual capabilities from your own code. The SDK APIs take a specification as input, so we recommend creating it with the help of an agent. You can add quality assessment to an existing process, generate data for a latest task, or combine several operations. You choose the preparation steps your project needs and how they fit into your model customization and evaluation processes.

Recent findings suggest that AI Data Preparation runs with an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role that you control. Your source data, generated datasets, and labels stay in your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets, in the AWS Region you choose.

Recent findings suggest that the AI data preparation capabilities are generally available in the US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions.

Recommended Practices CISA recommends customers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers.
  • Industry observers note that during the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work.
  • Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Industry observers note that during the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work. We expect this trend to continue as local AI and privacy become increasingly important in our everyday lives. Every fresh integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:.

In a recent development, we are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-consumers. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

In a recent development, the project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

Sources indicate that to reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

It has been revealed that we are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

Industry observers note that the llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

llama.cpp is nice but still needs improvement on huge prompt processing or aka prefill.

This is huge! Congratulations!!

View CSAF Summary The products listed below contain an authentication bypass vulnerability that could allow an on-path attacker to take over the session of a legitimate user and execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the victim user. Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. The following versions of Siemens SIMATIC are affected: SIMATIC BATCH V9.1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Information Server 2020 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Information Server 2022 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC PCS 7 V9.1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Process Historian 2020 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC Process Historian 2022 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V17 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V18 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V19 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V20 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC Runtime Professional V21 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC V7.5 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC V8.0 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) SIMATIC WinCC V8.1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-58114) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.5 Siemens SIMATIC BATCH V9.1 1 Vulnerability Weak Authentication Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-58114 Affected systems do not properly secure their remote user authentication with the deprecated NTLM protocol. This could allow unauthenticated remote attackers, who have achieved a machine in the middle position, to relay NTLM authentication and impersonate a legitimate user. The potential impact depends on the services that are accessible, e.g. a SQL server used by WinCC. View CSAF Summary On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to patch to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. #1174. Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2848 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, enterprises today need a clear way to extend their authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer, often requiring either broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets.
  • The core focus of this post is the outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, enterprises today need a clear way to extend their authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer, often requiring either broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead. When an AI agent running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model) needs to call the Snowflake-managed MCP server (which exposes Snowflake Cortex Agents as one of its tool types) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the first question enterprises must answer is: how does the agent authenticate? In this post, we walk through three Open Authorization (OAuth) configurations we tested on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Snowflake OAuth (per-user, no external Identity Provider, or IdP), three-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (corporate single sign-on, or SSO), and two-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (shared service user). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant (TOKEN_EXCHANGE) that delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt. We focus on the three configurations we tested end-to-end, flagging where OBO fits as we go. By the end, you will be able to identify which pattern suits your enterprise scenario.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets. It targets the Snowflake-managed MCP server, which surfaces Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as MCP tools that an MCP-aware client can discover and invoke. Rather than acting as a wrapper, the Gateway aggregates the capabilities of its configured targets into a single unified catalog, which it presents to the agent as one tools/list response.

The core focus of this post is the outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity acts as the credential broker: the Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT (because the Gateway uses JSON Web Token (JWT) inbound authentication), then calls GetResourceOauth2Token against the configured provider. AgentCore Identity owns the token vault, the token refresh, and the user-to-token binding, and it fetches, caches, and refreshes tokens automatically.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity supports three OAuth configurations spanning two grant types (authorization_code and client_credentials):.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also offers an API-key credential provider (which supports Snowflake Programmatic Access Tokens). We focus on OAuth here for per-user attribution and automatic token refresh. Each configuration uses a credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and a corresponding security integration on the Snowflake side.

Industry observers note that note: We tested these patterns with the Snowflake-managed MCP server using Okta and Microsoft Entra ID. Patterns 2 and 3 (external IdP) follow standard OAuth flows, so they can extend to other OAuth-protected MCP servers, but validate the token claims, scopes, and audience settings for your SaaS provider. Only Pattern 1 is Snowflake-specific, because it relies on Snowflake’s built-in OAuth authorization server. The Snowflake-specific elements are the OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER issuer-lock parameter, the session:role: / session:scope: grammar, BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST, LOGIN_NAME / EMAIL_ADDRESS mapping, and QUERY_HISTORY attribution. If your SaaS exposes its own internal OAuth server, you configure outbound OAuth the same way as Snowflake OAuth.

The following diagram shows the solution we built and the components it uses: a user-facing AI application, a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails redacting personally identifiable information (PII) from prompts and responses, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, over policy documents in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with the Snowflake-managed MCP server as its target, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity holding the token vault. The outbound OAuth path has the same shape in all three patterns: the Gateway resolves a token through AgentCore Identity, which obtains and renews it from an authorization server, and the Gateway then presents that token to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. What changes between the patterns is which authorization server challenges the token and under which grant: Snowflake’s own built-in OAuth server, or a third-party IdP. Those differences are set out in the Pattern comparison table, and each pattern’s runtime flow has its own sequence diagram later in this post.

Figure 1: Solution overview: the reference agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, combining Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Snowflake Cortex AI through the Snowflake-managed MCP server, and the authorization server that differs across the three OAuth patterns.

The following sections examine each pattern in detail: the authentication flow, configuration steps, and trade-offs to help you select the right approach for your use case.

Industry observers note that the Snowflake OAuth pattern uses a three-legged OAuth (3LO) flow to deliver per-user authentication without requiring an external identity provider. Each user authenticates to Snowflake with their own credentials, consents to a specific Snowflake role, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity caches that user’s access and refresh tokens. Every subsequent Snowflake call executes as that user, and QUERY_HISTORY records their real username. Note that per-role consent is not the default. The Snowflake-managed MCP server advertises session:role:all and falls back to DEFAULT_ROLE, so you set OAUTH_SCOPES_SUPPORTED (an account-, database-, or schema-level parameter set with ALTER) to narrow the role scope the server advertises, and restrict ALLOWED_ROLES_LIST on the integration to enforce which roles a user can consent to (PRE_AUTHORIZED_ROLES_LIST does the opposite: it lists roles that skip the consent step).

What makes this pattern appealing is its simplicity: no external identity provider is required. Snowflake acts as both the authorization server and the resource server, exposing its own built-in OAuth endpoints (/oauth/authorize and /oauth/token-request). Setup follows a specific order, because the callback URL does not exist until the credential provider is created. The administrator first creates the CustomOauth2 credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity with placeholder client credentials and records the callbackUrl that AgentCore Identity returns. That callbackUrl is then registered as the redirect URI on a Snowflake security integration created with TYPE = OAUTH and OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM. Finally, the administrator updates the credential provider with the real client ID and secret issued by Snowflake and configures the provider’s oauthDiscovery with explicit authorization server metadata: the issuer (the Snowflake account URL), the authorization endpoint (/oauth/authorize), and the token endpoint (/oauth/token-request).

The following screenshot indicates the configuration steps for credential provider vendors in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity with Snowflake OAuth (3LO) settings.

Figure 2: Configuring the Snowflake OAuth (3LO) credential provider vendor in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity.

Next, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration points to the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and references the custom Snowflake OAuth for outbound authentication.

Figure 3: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration pointing to the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and Snowflake OAuth (3LO) as outbound auth.

The following sequence diagram shows the runtime authorization flow for the Snowflake OAuth pattern.

Figure 4: Snowflake OAuth (3LO) runtime authorization flow: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway MCP server target with AUTHORIZATION_CODE grant, per-user Snowflake OAuth, and session:role:ANALYST_ROLE scope.

The Snowflake OAuth authorization flow works as follows:.

Recent findings suggest that access tokens are short-lived. By default, they last 600 seconds (maximum 3600). When an access token expires, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity automatically uses the refresh token to obtain a upcoming access token, with no user interaction required. If the security integration is configured to prevent refreshing tokens, the user must re-authorize through the consent screen. Refresh-token lifetime is controlled by OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_VALIDITY. The reference implementation sets it to 86400 seconds (1 day), and Snowflake allows up to 90 days. OAUTH_ISSUE_REFRESH_TOKENS (default TRUE) governs whether refresh tokens are issued at all.

According to recent reports, note: By default, Snowflake helps prevent the ACCOUNTADMIN, ORGADMIN, GLOBALORGADMIN, and SECURITYADMIN roles from being used with OAuth integrations. This is controlled by BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST for Snowflake OAuth (and EXTERNAL_OAUTH_BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST for External OAuth), applies to all three patterns, and covers the primary role only. With OAUTH_USE_SECONDARY_ROLES = IMPLICIT, secondary roles can still carry these privileged roles.

The Snowflake OAuth pattern is the simplest path to per-user audit trails. It needs no external IdP configuration and no additional vendor dependency. It is best suited for scenarios where:.

This pattern combines per-user authentication with corporate single sign-on. Users sign in through the external IdP, which enforces multi-factor authentication (MFA), conditional access, and session policies. The IdP-issued JWT is presented to Snowflake, which validates it through its External OAuth security integration (optionally issuer-locked to the MCP server’s schema, database, or account with OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER). Snowflake verifies the issuer, audience, and signature through a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS). It then maps a configurable claim, set with EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TOKEN_USER_MAPPING_CLAIM (sub for Okta, upn for Microsoft Entra ID), to a Snowflake user’s LOGIN_NAME or EMAIL_ADDRESS (with EXTERNAL_OAUTH_SNOWFLAKE_USER_MAPPING_ATTRIBUTE), and runs the query as that user. The security integration parameter values are case-sensitive.

It has been revealed that the key difference from Pattern 1: the authorization server is your corporate IdP (such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID), not Snowflake. Snowflake remains the resource server. Users authenticate with the same credentials and policies they use for every other corporate application. No separate Snowflake passwords are required.

Recent findings suggest that on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore side, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity provides built-in credential provider vendors for popular identity providers (for example, OktaOauth2 and MicrosoftOauth2). These vendors accept the client ID, client secret, and IdP endpoints through includedOauth2ProviderConfig, compared to the generic CustomOauth2 provider used in Pattern 1. The Snowflake-managed MCP server uses pre-registered OAuth clients, so you register each client ID and secret in advance, which is why the create, record callbackUrl, register, enhancement sequence is required.

Figure 5: Configuring the Okta OAuth (3-legged) credential provider vendor in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity.

Next, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration points to the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and references the Okta credential provider for outbound authentication.

Figure 6: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration pointing to the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint with Okta 3-legged OAuth as outbound authentication.

The following sequence diagram indicates the runtime authorization flow for the three-legged OAuth pattern with an external IdP.

Figure 7: 3LO with external IdP runtime authorization flow: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway MCP server target with AUTHORIZATION_CODE grant and third-party IdP outbound auth.

Snowflake’s External OAuth security integration flow works as follows:.

Token lifetime governance: Unlike Pattern 1 where Snowflake controls token lifetimes, access token and refresh token lifetimes are governed by the IdP, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity handles the refresh transparently. If a refresh token was issued, the user re-authenticates only when it expires, based on the IdP’s session policy. Otherwise, the user re-authenticates when the access token expires.

Choose three-legged OAuth (3LO) with a third-party IdP when:.

The two-legged OAuth pattern uses the OAuth 2.0 client_credentials grant. This is a machine-to-machine flow with no user interaction. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity obtains a JWT from the IdP using the configured client ID and client secret, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway presents it to Snowflake, which executes the requests under a shared service user, regardless of which end user initiated the query.

This pattern is the most operationally direct: no consent screens, no per-user token vaults, no browser redirects. The owners follow the same code path. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity fetches and caches the client_credentials token automatically, and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway presents it on every outbound call to the Snowflake-managed MCP server.

The key difference from Patterns 1 and 2: there is no per-user identity propagation. Snowflake’s QUERY_HISTORY records a single service user for queries. The trade-off is operational simplicity at the cost of per-user audit granularity. On the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore side, the credential provider uses the client_credentials grant type: either a built-in vendor (OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) or the generic CustomOauth2 provider. Configuration requires the IdP’s token endpoint, client ID, and client secret. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity fetches a token from the IdP on the first tool call (when the Gateway calls GetResourceOauth2Token), caches it, and, because client_credentials challenges no refresh token, requests a fresh one before expiry. No agent-level code changes are required.

Figure 8: Configuring the client_credentials (2-legged) credential provider vendor in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity.

Next, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration references the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and the two-legged OAuth credential provider for outbound authentication.

Figure 9: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration pointing to the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint with 2-legged OAuth (client_credentials) as outbound authentication.

The following sequence diagram demonstrates the runtime authorization flow for the two-legged OAuth pattern.

Figure 10: 2LO with external IdP runtime authorization flow: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway MCP server target with CLIENT_CREDENTIALS grant and third-party IdP outbound auth.

Snowflake’s External OAuth security integration 2LO flow works as follows:.

Because the two-legged OAuth target needs no user consent, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway connects to the Snowflake-managed MCP server at target-creation time and discovers tools through implicit sync during target creation. In the 3-legged OAuth patterns (Patterns 1 and 2), the Gateway target supports two creation methods: (1) an admin completes the authorization code flow so tools are discovered by implicit sync, or (2) the admin provides the tool schema upfront. (Discovery behavior is a ListingMode property of the target, not a property of the grant type.).

The two-legged OAuth pattern is preferred for automated, unattended, and batch workloads. It is ideal when:.

¹ MCP protocol revision: for the three-legged patterns (Patterns 1 and 2), the gateway pins 2025-11-25 in its supported MCP revisions, which the URL-mode elicitation (-32042) handshake requires. The reference 2LO gateway (Pattern 3) does not pin it, because 2LO has no elicitation step. On accounts that are not enabled for MCP version updates, the supported set is fixed when the gateway is created.

² Works unattended: Patterns 1 and 2 run unattended only until the refresh token expires. Re-consent then requires a live browser, the same user, and completion inside the 10-minute authorization window (CompleteResourceTokenAuth), which is why 3LO is unsuitable for fully unattended scheduled jobs. Pattern 3 (2LO) has no refresh token and no consent step, so it runs unattended indefinitely.

The three configurations in this post cover two grant types: authorization_code (Patterns 1 and 2) and client_credentials (Pattern 3). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange (TOKEN_EXCHANGE), which delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt.

It has been revealed that OBO exchanges an inbound user token for a Snowflake-scoped token that preserves the real user’s identity, so QUERY_HISTORY attributes each query to the actual user, while keeping the unattended, machine-to-machine flow of Pattern 3 (no browser redirect, no consent screen). On the Snowflake side it uses the same TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH integration as Patterns 2 and 3 (optionally issuer-locked with OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER). On the AgentCore side it is configured on the OAuth credential provider through onBehalfOfTokenExchangeConfig (grant mode TOKEN_EXCHANGE for Okta/RFC 8693, or JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT for Microsoft Entra). OBO uses the External OAuth path (Patterns 2 and 3).

OBO is generally available on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, but it was outside the scope of the three configurations we tested for this post.

Industry observers note that to see these patterns in action, we built a financial-services credit-risk assessment agent as a reference workload. A single agent combines bank policy documents in Amazon S3 (through Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases) with customer data in Snowflake. It assesses loan eligibility, searches customer profiles, and queries account and transaction data. The demo exercises three MCP tools (Cortex Search, Cortex Analyst, and SQL Execution) across all three OAuth configurations for side-by-side comparison in your own AWS account.

It has been revealed that though the demo is financial services, the patterns work across healthcare, supply chain, insurance, and more. All three implementations are public and deploy end-to-end through a single deploy.sh script:.

Recent findings suggest that note: For demonstration purposes, the reference implementations expose SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL on the same MCP server as the Cortex Agent. Snowflake recommends exposing a Cortex Agent as the only client-facing tool for governed business questions. If direct SQL is required, place it on a separate MCP server with a dedicated least-privileged role.

In this post, we walked through three OAuth configurations for authenticating AI agents to Snowflake Cortex AI over MCP through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Snowflake OAuth offers the simplest path to per-user audit trails with no external IdP dependency. Three-legged OAuth with an external IdP adds corporate SSO, centralized MFA, and conditional access while preserving per-user identity. Two-legged OAuth with an external IdP serves machine-to-machine through a shared service user.

Across all three patterns, the agent code and the Snowflake MCP tool set stay unchanged. The OAuth wiring differs in four specific ways:.

Beyond these four, only the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity credential provider (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and the Snowflake security integration differ. Understanding these differences in grant type, token issuance, user mapping, and audit behavior equips you to select the right OAuth configuration for your compliance, operational, and user-experience needs.

To get started, explore the reference implementation in our GitHub repository. For more on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore service detail page or the Developer Guide.

#1165. Latest Update: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1203 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help people who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail.
  • A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y.
  • Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help people who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

Recent findings suggest that the models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer consumers away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

In a recent development, people use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when people don't know the right questions to ask.

Sources indicate that we built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

Sources indicate that for the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

Recent findings suggest that A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

According to recent reports, A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:.

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

In a recent development, A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

It has been revealed that we also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

It has been revealed that A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Industry observers note that researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Sources indicate that future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench at the moment covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#1163. Latest Update: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2013 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them.
  • Recent findings suggest that custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry.
  • According to recent reports, in this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them. AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog for registering, approving, and discovering these resources and custom records. Each record carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. However, every organization has attributes and facts that it wants to track, and some are unique to that organization, such as its business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments. Organizations want one common definition for each of these attributes, and they want every agent, MCP server, and skill in the registry to carry these facts. Until now, organizations had no way to define these facts in AWS Agent Registry and store them on each record.

Recent findings suggest that custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs that records in an AWS Agent Registry carry. An administrator defines the schema and applies it to the registry, and all records within the registry must then adhere to the schema. When publishers create or submit records, they supply values for the fields specified in the applicable schema, and AWS Agent Registry validates those values against the schema set by the admin. Approvers can rely on the validated values when reviewing a record, and consumers and agents can use them to discover and filter records. Administrators, publishers, security and governance teams, approvers, consumers, and agents all work from a shared set of facts to govern, discover, and understand the resources in their agentic fleet.

According to recent reports, in this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents. We use an MCP server as the example, but the same steps apply to other record types.

With custom metadata, an organization can use standardized vocabulary for describing its resources. The registry administrator defines the custom metadata schema: field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional. The registry enforces the schema on every record, so a field such as environment has the same name and the same allowed values whichever team publishes the record.

The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and you can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types. Each field is Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean.

When a record is created or updated, the registry validates the custom metadata against the schema set up by the admin.

If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as NON_COMPLIANT. A team can save work in progress this way, but it can’t submit the record for approval until it has the required fields and values.

If a record includes custom metadata with an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, AWS Agent Registry rejects it with a ValidationException.

GetRegistryRecord returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status. (COMPLIANT means that the values match the administrator’s schema. It is not an approval. The approvers make that decision.).

Discovery APIs also allow filtering records based on custom attributes.

Because teams can describe the AWS Agent Registry records with the same fields and values, the registry can support and scale governance and compliance.

Sources indicate that fields such as environment (prod, staging, or dev), businessUnit, ownerTeam, supportContact, and costCenter record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it. A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to your existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for anyone who depends on the resource.

Data classification, compliance scope such as Payment Card Industry (PCI) or Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), risk tier, scan status, and a scan report URL turn an approval into a check of structured evidence. Your existing scanners, CMDB sync jobs, and classification tools write these values through the API before a record is submitted. You can build your record approval process or automation using these values, as this post shows.

Sources indicate that custom metadata values are indexed for search. A consumer or agent can combine a natural-language query with specific metadata filters, such as environment=prod AND businessUnit=payments AND securityScanStatus=PASSED. Only approved records are returned, so a record that matches the filters but hasn’t been approved stays out of the results. Figure 1 reveals how each role, from administrator to consumer, moves a record through schema definition, registration, enrichment, approval, and discovery.

Figure 1: Swimlane diagram showing how a record moves through AWS Agent Registry, by role.

In a recent development, anyCompany operates anycompany-governed-registry, an AWS Agent Registry without auto-approval. Its payments team publishes an MCP record, payments-ledger-mcp, a read-only server for ledger lookups. Existing security and inventory systems enrich this MCP record before an approval function decides whether consumers can discover it.

The five numbered steps in Figure 2 match the walkthrough: define, register, enrich and submit, review, then discover.

Figure 2: Custom metadata gathers publisher context and values from your existing tools, so approval and search can use the same facts.

To follow the walkthrough, you need:.

An AWS account in a supported AWS Region.

AWS credentials available to Boto3 and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for AWS Agent Registry.

Python 3.11 or later and boto3 1.43.113 or later.

The sample implementation is in the GitHub repo.

According to recent reports, the snippets are shortened: cp and dp are the agent-registry-control and agent-registry boto3 clients. The sample repository has the complete code.

AnyCompany’s admin creates a registry with a custom metadata schema that every record must follow.

Every record must have its environment, businessUnit, and securityScanStatus fields.

Records can also carry optional fields that the publisher or automation fills in later: ownerTeam, cmdbId, dataClassification, and securityScanReportUrl.

MCP servers also record their networkEgress, which is optional.

Figure 3 reveals this schema and the values payments-ledger-mcp will carry once enrichment completes in Step 3. The empty autoApprovalRules list means that the registry approves nothing on its own. Every submitted record stays in Pending approval until someone or something approves it. You decide whether that is done by automated checks you build (Step 4 uses an AWS Lambda function), a human approver, or both.

Figure 3: Diagram showing the registry’s common attributes, the fields added for MCP records, and the validated customMetadata map for payments-ledger-mcp.

It has been revealed that administrators can also review the schema in the AWS Agent Registry console. Figure 4 reveals the common attributes and the MCP-specific field as they appear on the registry’s details page.

Figure 4: The custom metadata schema in the AWS Agent Registry console.

The payments team’s pipeline registers payments-ledger-mcp with its custom metadata. Its first attempt uses production instead of one of the administrator’s allowed values.

The registry rejects the record. After the pipeline sends prod, the record is created as a compliant draft. This is how the schema keeps every team using the same values.

Next, AnyCompany’s automation adds what its own systems know: the result from its security scanner, the asset ID from its CMDB, and the approved data classification. It then submits the record for approval.

An update replaces the whole metadata map, so the automation reads the current values, adds its own, and writes them back together. In the sample, the scanner and CMDB calls are stubs that you replace with your own tools. The registry sends a pending-approval event to Amazon EventBridge. In Step 4, a rule that you create passes the event to your approval function.

When the record moves to Pending approval, AWS Agent Registry sends an event to Amazon EventBridge, and an Amazon EventBridge rule is set to invoke a custom AWS Lambda function. Figure 5 shows the console view of payments-ledger-mcp, with the custom metadata values that the approval function reads for its check.

Figure 5: The custom metadata on the record is the evidence that the approval function will check.

The function reads the record’s custom metadata and compliance status to check that the record is COMPLIANT, the scan PASSED, a cmdbId is present, and the data is public or internal. payments-ledger-mcp passes all four, so the function approves. A record that fails a check is rejected, and the reason names the failed check. In your production systems, you can choose to route records that need a human review, such as those with confidential or restricted data, for manual review instead of being rejected.

A developer looking for a ledger tool searches the registry and filters on the same fields the administrator defined.

Industry observers note that the search returns payments-ledger-mcp because it’s approved and matches all three filters. Agents can run the same search through the registry’s MCP endpoint, https://agentregistry..api.aws/registry//mcp, which offers search, list, and get as MCP tools. In the GitHub sample, a Strands agent connects to the AWS Registry MCP endpoint and uses a model on Amazon Bedrock. Its system prompt lists the custom metadata fields to filter records on. The agent turns a plain-language request, such as “a production MCP server for payments ledger lookups that passed its security scan”, into a filtered search. It answers with payments-ledger-mcp.

Developers and agents query the same fields the administrator defined, and the approval function checked, so both find only servers that meet your governance rules.

Treat the schema as your organization’s shared vocabulary:.

Agree on the vocabulary first. Settle field names and allowed values with the teams that publish and approve records before you create the schema. Schema changes are additive: you can add fields, add allowed values, or make an optional field required, but you can’t rename, remove, or retype a field.

Expect existing records to lag behind schema changes made after the records were added to the registry. Existing records aren’t rewritten. A record that no longer matches the schema is reported as NON_COMPLIANT and keeps its approval status. The record stays approved, but its next upgrade must meet the latest schema. Editing an approved record creates a draft that must be submitted for approval again, and the submit fails until every required field has a value. Until a curator approves the new revision, consumers keep seeing the approved one.

Put each field at the right level. Use common attributes for questions that apply to every record type, and record-type fields for record-specific facts such as autonomy level for agents.

In a recent development, pick the type that fits the field. Use Enums for decision fields that need consistent spelling, Text for external identifiers, and URL for evidence stored behind the source system’s access controls.

According to recent reports, make a field required only when the publisher can assign a value at registration. For a value that your continuous integration (CI) or automation provides after the record is published, allow an interim value, for example PENDING. In this post, the scan runs after registration, so securityScanStatus has three values: PENDING, PASSED, and FAILED. The publisher writes PENDING, and the enrichment automation replaces it.

Keep sensitive details out. Leave secrets, internal endpoints, and detailed findings out of broadly readable metadata.

It has been revealed that in this post, we demonstrated how to add custom metadata in AWS Agent Registry to give every record a common set of facts, such as its environment, owning business unit, data classification, and security scan status. Using one MCP server, we showed an administrator defining the schema, a publisher and existing automation filling in the values, an approval function that you build in AWS Lambda deciding approval, and a consumer finding the approved server with metadata filters. Because the administrator owns the schema, every team uses the same fields and values, and that consistency is what makes approvals and searches in AWS Agent Registry dependable.

Try it yourself: Use the sample at GitHub repo.

Go deeper: Read the AWS Agent Registry Developer Guide and custom metadata API reference.

The following versions of Dorsett Controls InfoScan are affected: InfoScan <=1.45.0 (CVE-2026-117659, CVE-2026-120157, CVE-2026-120255, CVE-2026-120260, CVE-2026-120271, CVE-2026-120298) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.1 Dorsett Controls InfoScan 5 Vulnerabilities Improper Certificate Validation, Exposure of Sensitive System Information to an Unauthorized Control Sphere, Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key, Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Water and Wastewater Systems Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-117659 The InfoScan Electron desktop client improperly handles TLS certificate errors by accepting certificates without validating their trustworthiness. The client also configures Electron with nodeIntegration enabled, contextIsolation disabled, and webSecurity disabled. These settings weaken the client’s security boundaries. An attacker who is able to intercept or manipulate network communications may be able to present an untrusted certificate without the application rejecting the connection. Recommended Practices CISA recommends consumers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets
