⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.
  • Industry observers note that for robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives.
  • SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

Industry observers note that for robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:.

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Industry observers note that figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

According to recent reports, A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

Industry observers note that during pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

Industry observers note that this example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Sources indicate that open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

In a recent development, use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

Industry observers note that the arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

Sources indicate that simReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:.

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

In a recent development, confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

According to recent reports, you can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:.

Sample prompt used in this example:.

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

In a recent development, with the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Sample prompt used in this example:.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’.

Recent findings suggest that the full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

According to recent reports, if your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

It has been revealed that these results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

It has been revealed that what will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that view CSAF Summary Fortinet has published information on a Double Free vulnerability in FortiOS. This advisory lists the related Siemens Industrial products. Siemens recommends to enhancement Fortigate NGFW to V7.6.9 or later following the secure update recommendation procedure. Contact customer support to receive detailed information The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 are affected: RUGGEDCOM APE1808 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-106175) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 2.3 Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 1 Vulnerability Double Free Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Organization Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-106175 A Double Free vulnerability [CWE-415] in FortiOS, FortiProxy and FortiSwitch may allow a local authenticated attacker to crash the newcli daemon via crafted CLI commands. Read More 1 Affected Product RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Fortinet NGFW Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixUpdate Fortigate NGFW to V7.6.9 or later following the secure update recommendation procedure. Contact customer support to receive detailed information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-415 Double Free CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 2.3 LOW CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L View CVE Details Acknowledgments Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Susana Barraza is the NICE Program Manager at NIST. She previously served as the Student Personnel Assistant for the HSI STEM Equity and Success Initiative (SESI) Project at Sacramento City College. She has also participated in a Political Management Seminar at The George Washington University as a component of a fellowship with the Congressional Hispanic Leadership Institute in Washington, DC. Additionally, Susana served as an intern for Ford Motor Firm, the House of Representatives, and for the California State Assembly.

Recent findings suggest that susana earned an Associates of Science in Business Administration and an Associates of Arts in Interdisciplinary Studies- Social and Behavioral Sciences. Then Susana transferred to California State University, Sacramento (CSUS) where she received a Bachelor’s in Economics with a minor in Business Administration. She is a 2020 Pathway Fellow Recipient with the College of Education at CSUS; a program (1 out of 6 nationwide) that prepares highly qualified diverse participants for doctorates and careers in rigorous educational research. In 2026, Susana completed a Master's in education, with a focus on organizational leadership and learning at The George Washington University.

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

Industry observers note that the router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

Sources indicate that the same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise aims include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

According to recent reports, the best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

In a recent development, openRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million customers, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

Industry observers note that when a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

It has been revealed that pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO owners get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

It has been revealed that on model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two upcoming tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:.

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

Industry observers note that in your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

In a recent development, requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

Sources indicate that this is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:.

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

View CSAF Summary .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API contains multiple vulnerabilities that could allow an attacker to obtain sensitive information or write arbitrary files outside the intended download directory. Siemens has released a newly introduced version for .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API and recommends to revision to the latest version. The following versions of Siemens .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API are affected: .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API vers:intdot/<3.3.61, vers:intdot/<3.3.62 (CVE-2026-85114, CVE-2026-85115) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.5 Siemens .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API 2 Vulnerabilities Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal'), Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-85114 Affected applications do not properly validate filenames received from remote servers during ticket downloads. This could allow an attacker who can manipulate the ticket response to write arbitrary files outside the intended download directory and, when overwriting is enabled, replace existing files accessible to the application. Read More 1 Affected Product .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API < V3.3.61 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixUpdate to V3.3.61 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.5 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N View CVE Details CVE-2026-85115 Affected applications do not properly redact PLC restore passwords from HTTP error exception messages. This could allow an attacker with access to logs or other diagnostic output to obtain the plaintext restore password and potentially perform unauthorized operations on the PLC. Read More 2 Affected Products .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API < V3.3.61 Product Status: known_affected Remediations .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API < V3.3.62 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixUpdate to V3.3.62 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-209 Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 5.5 MEDIUM CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments Siemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends consumers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.
